meta.name: rq3-association-rules
meta.description:
Mine association rules on the earlier baskets, measure them unchanged on the
later ones, and report what share still holds.
meta.author: Saurabh Singh

notes: Return lines were excluded. A return is the reversal of a purchase decision, not a second one, and a credit note listing six items is not evidence that those six go together.

Excluded 12 non-product codes imported from preprocessing.field_guide. Postage and bank charges co-occur with almost everything, so left in they produce the highest-lift rules in the dataset and every one of them is an artefact of billing.
Single-item baskets were kept. They cannot contribute to a rule, but they belong in the denominator: support is the share of all baskets, and dropping them would inflate every support figure.

split.method: Chronological. A random split would put baskets from the same week on both sides, confirming a seasonal pairing with data a few days from the baskets that produced it.

itemsets.pruning_note: Downward closure removed 1,259 candidates before they were counted; 248,162 were counted. Without the pruning every candidate would have had to be counted.

rules_summary.note: 1,148 of 1,148 rules survived the false-discovery-rate correction. The correction rejected nothing: every rule significant at the raw threshold stayed significant after it. That means these associations sit far from the threshold, not that the correction was unnecessary - it had to be applied to know.

redundant.note: 42 of 1,148 rules were restatements of a more general rule with the same consequent and within 5% of the same confidence. They are true but add nothing, and leaving them in would make one finding look like several.

validated_set: Associations only - rules with lift above 1 that survived the false-discovery-rate correction, with restatements of more general rules removed. Rules that cleared the support and confidence thresholds but failed their own significance test are counted in rules_generated and excluded here, because nobody would act on them and their presence would turn the survival rate into a measure of how much noise the thresholds admitted.

holdout_validation.verdict: 100.0% of rules still hold on baskets they were not mined on. The associations describe the business rather than the mining window, and acting on the stronger ones is defensible. The lift ranking is preserved across periods (Spearman 0.95).
holdout_validation.method_note: Rules were mined on the earlier baskets and recomputed, unchanged, on 9,882 later ones. Nothing was refitted. Surviving required both lift above 1.0 and significance at alpha = 0.05 after a Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the 1,100 rules judged; 0 rules cleared the lift threshold but not the test, which is what independence looks like when it lands fractionally above 1.0 by chance. Rules whose antecedent occurs fewer than 5 times in the hold-out are excluded from the rate rather than counted either way.

rule_set_overlap.note: Mining the two periods independently produced top-50 lists sharing 13 rules (Jaccard 0.15). This measures whether the method finds the same rules again, which is a different question from whether a given rule stayed true.

recommender_hazards.source: Kathriarachchi, Alam & Rashid (2026), ACM Transactions on Recommender Systems 4(3), Article 42, section 4.2.

item_coverage.verdict: 4.0% of the catalogue can ever be recommended (187 of 4,734 products). The remaining 96.0% never clears minimum support, so no rule reaches them however a customer behaves. This is the popularity bias of Kathriarachchi et al. (2026) §3.2 measured rather than asserted, and it is a property of the support threshold, not a defect in the data.

new_item_coverage.verdict: 0.0% of the 319 products new to the hold-out window can be recommended by rules mined before they existed. A rule can only name products present when it was mined, so this is a structural limit of association rules rather than a result about this dataset: every new product is invisible to the method until the rules are mined again.

transparency.verdict: Every recommendation an association rule makes carries its own explanation - the antecedent, the support count and the confidence - so the transparency index of Kathriarachchi et al. (2026) Equation 12 is 1.0 by construction. Their synthetic example scores 0.500. This is the dimension on which a rule-based recommender beats a latent-factor model outright, and it is worth stating beside the coverage results.

exposure_concentration.note: Gini 0.657 across 187 recommendable products; the most recommended tenth of them account for 56.0% of all recommendation opportunities. 0 would be perfectly even exposure and 1 all exposure on one product.

not_computable.why_not: Online Retail II has a pseudonymous Customer ID and a country, and no demographic attribute. Country is a market, not a protected characteristic, and reporting it as one would misrepresent both the data and the hazard.
Their definition estimates it by training an attack model against recommendation logs. There are no logs - nothing has been deployed - and no attribute to infer.
The dataset carries no reviews or ratings to be faked.
There are no ratings in the dataset.

not_computable.needs: demographic groups and a decision threshold
not_computable.why_not: Same missing field as the bias ratio.

not_computable.needs: ground-truth relevance for precision at k
not_computable.why_not: Precision needs to know whether a recommendation was right, which needs either a deployment or labelled relevance. The coverage term of the same equation IS computed here; the composite is not, because two of its three terms would be invented.
The dataset has product descriptions, not content claims.
Same missing field as the bias ratio.

recommender_hazards.count_rec_note: count_rec(i) is taken as the number of rules in which item i is a consequent. Their definition counts recommendation slots served to users; nothing is deployed here, so this is the closest available analogue and is reported as a substitution, not as their measure applied unchanged.

singleton_policy.source: Qiu, Ning, Zhang & Yang (2023), ICMLCA 2023, sections 3.1-3.2 and Tables 2, 10 and 11.
singleton_policy.verdict: Removing 3,221 single-item baskets (8.1% of the data) changed the rule count from 815 to 1,007 at identical thresholds. Of the rules present in both runs, 815 had an unchanged support count but a higher support figure - the same baskets, divided by a smaller denominator. Qiu et al. (2023) report the larger rule count as an improvement; on this data it is at least partly an artefact of the denominator, and the chapter should say which it is rather than adopting their framing.

colocation.verdict: A rule-driven grouping needs 17.15 zone visits per order on average, and 8.8% of orders can be filled from a single zone. That is 20.3% fewer than random assignment and 3.3% fewer than grouping by popularity alone.
colocation.method_note: Jirapatsil & Phumchusri (2022) report a 54.4% reduction in average picking distance after rearranging a known warehouse. Online Retail II carries no layout, so distance in metres cannot be computed and is not reported. The quantity here is the number of distinct storage zones a picker must visit per historical order, which is what a layout is chosen to minimise and is derived entirely from the data. The percentages are against the stated baselines, not against a previous real layout, so they are not comparable to their 54.4%.

sources.support_confidence_lift: Jirapatsil & Phumchusri (2022), MSIE 2022, Equations 1-5; the lift > 1 decision rule is their section 3.1.
sources.dependence_measures: Ni, Luo, Lu & Zhu (2020), ACM TMIS 11(1) Article 3, Equations 3, 4, 8 and 10.
sources.singleton_deletion: Qiu, Ning, Zhang & Yang (2023), ICMLCA 2023, sections 3.1-3.2, replicated and examined rather than adopted.
sources.hazard_metrics: Kathriarachchi, Alam & Rashid (2026), ACM TORS 4(3) Article 42, Equations 4, 10 and 12.
sources.colocation: Jirapatsil & Phumchusri (2022), MSIE 2022, section 3.2. Their distance reduction is not reproduced; see colocation.method_note.
sources.not_from_the_supplied_papers: Leverage, conviction and Zhang's metric; the chronological hold-out validation; and the Benjamini-Hochberg correction. The Fisher exact test itself follows the chi-square dependence testing of Silverstein et al. (1998) as described in Ni et al. (2020) section 2.4.
